intro:
This is the audio overview of the GenAI guide, written for a React developer who is asked to build features on top of large language models. It follows one worked example all the way through: a user picks three insurance quotes and asks the application to compare them. The carriers, prices and rules in that example are invented for practice.

The guide has fourteen sections. A start here explainer, a cheatsheet, model foundations, the worked comparison flow, retrieval and vectors, tools and agents, conversation features, React integration, prompts and safety, evaluation, production, tools and providers, React essentials, and how to answer well.

One idea holds the guide together. Facts come from systems of record, decisions come from code, and only the wording comes from the model.

chapters.title: Start Here: GenAI Explained
chapters.text:
The first section is the start here explainer, the whole guide in about an hour and a quarter of reading. Here is its outline.

How a model works. Text is split into tokens, and pricing, limits and latency are all counted per token. The model predicts the next token, again and again.

Prompts and structured output. A prompt is a specification: the role and task, the boundary between data and instructions, the shape of the output, and what to do when the evidence is missing.

Embeddings. An embedding is a fixed length vector produced by an embedding model, and texts with similar meaning land close together. It is not a copy of the text.

Retrieval augmented generation, or RAG. Retrieval finds the relevant text, and the model answers from it and cites it. The prompt contains retrieved text, never vectors.

Tool calling. The model asks, and your code acts. The model returns a request to call a function with arguments. Your backend validates it, runs it and sends the result back.

Workflows and agents. In a workflow, code decides the steps. Start there whenever the intent is known. In an agent, the model picks the next allowed tool.

Streaming to React. The browser never holds the provider's key. React calls your route, and the route authenticates, validates, orchestrates and streams.

Safety. A document or a tool result can contain instructions. Treat it as data.

Evaluation. Changing chunking, filters or prompts is application tuning. Fine tuning trains the model's weights. Only say fine tuned if you did that.

And production, where the failures to name are provider errors, a timeout from one source, and a stream that disconnects.

chapters.title: Cheatsheet
chapters.text:
The second section is a cheatsheet, made for a last pass before an interview. It has four parts.

The first is a one page map organised around a single question: where does each kind of information come from? Exact facts, such as prices, limits and expiry dates, come from your APIs and database. That is an ordinary read. It is not tool calling in itself. Policy wording comes from retrieval, as text with source ids. Decisions come from versioned rules in code. And the explanation, the wording, comes from the model.

The second part is six distinctions to say precisely, because interviewers use them to test real understanding. An API call against tool calling: a tool is a capability the model may ask for, and it can wrap an API. Retrieval against fine tuning: one supplies knowledge at request time, the other changes the model's behaviour. A workflow against an agent: who decides the next step, your code or the model. Application tuning against fine tuning. An embedding against the text it came from. And streaming against a complete response.

The third part is a glossary, one plain line per term: token, context window, temperature, embedding, chunk, top k, reranking, grounding, hallucination, guardrail.

The fourth is a list of facts, versions and API names, each checked against official documentation on a stated date. The lesson there is about habit more than content. Library and provider APIs change quickly, so before an interview, and before you write code, check the installed versions and the current documentation, and do not trust an older tutorial.

chapters.title: LLM Foundations
chapters.text:
Section three is model foundations.

A large language model is a neural network, a transformer, trained to predict the next token of text. Given everything in its context window, it outputs probabilities for the next token, picks one, and repeats. It is not looking anything up.

Tokens are the units it reads and writes: whole words, pieces of words, punctuation. The context window is how many tokens it can consider at once, and it covers both the input and the output.

At the level an application engineer needs, a transformer turns each token into a vector, and then uses self attention, where for every token the model works out how much each other token matters to it.

Three settings shape the output. Temperature scales the probabilities: low values make the answer more repeatable, high values more varied. Top p limits the choice to the most likely tokens. And max tokens caps the length.

Why do models hallucinate? Because they are trained to produce plausible continuations, not to check facts. When the context lacks the answer, the most plausible continuation can still be wrong. What reduces it is supplying the evidence, allowing the model to say it does not know, and validating the output.

Which lever fixes which problem? Start with the cheapest that addresses the actual failure. Prompts and a schema for format. Retrieval for knowledge. Tools for live data and actions. And fine tuning for persistent behaviour or style. Fine tuning is a poor way to add facts that change often.

Reasoning models think before they answer, and do better on problems with several steps, at a cost in time and tokens. And prompt caching is a provider feature that makes a repeated prefix cheaper. It is not the same as caching answers.

chapters.title: Worked Example: AI Quote Comparison
chapters.text:
Section four is the worked example, and it is the heart of the guide.

The user has selected three quotes and asks for a comparison, with requirements such as a deductible no higher than five hundred dollars and rental coverage included.

The forty five second architecture answer goes like this. React sends the quote ids and the coverage preferences to a Node endpoint. The backend authenticates the user, and checks that these quotes belong to them. It loads the exact facts from the quote systems. It retrieves the relevant policy wording as evidence. It applies the rules and scores the quotes in code. It asks the model to explain the result. And it validates that explanation before streaming it back. In short: ids, authorisation, facts, evidence, score, explanation, validation.

Hard constraints come before the score. Eligibility is checked first, with deterministic rules and no model call. A quote with a thousand dollar deductible fails the five hundred dollar limit, however cheap it is. Price is a preference that only applies among the quotes that pass.

A common mix up is to picture tool calling as a separate step in a pipeline. In this design the backend already knows what to fetch, so it is a plain workflow. Tool calling matters when the model must decide what to fetch.

Then the failure cases. If one carrier times out, return the available quotes and mark that carrier as unavailable. Never invent its numbers. If a document does not mention rental coverage, represent that as unknown. Do not turn absence of evidence into not covered.

And should you compare with retrieval or with a database? Both, for different data. Direct reads for current prices and limits. Retrieval for policy wording.

chapters.title: RAG & Vectors
chapters.text:
Section five is retrieval and vectors.

RAG is a retrieval pipeline plus generation, and you should be able to explain both halves.

The offline half is ingestion. Start from approved content. Extract the text, split it into chunks, attach metadata such as the policy version and the tenant, compute an embedding for each chunk, and store it. And keep it current: when a document changes, its chunks are replaced.

The online half answers one question. Resolve what is actually being asked, using the conversation. Does the second one include rental needs the selected quote and its policy id, not a search of everything. Embed the question with the same embedding model. Search within the authorised scope. Then build the prompt from the retrieved text.

Know one chunking failure. A chunk says rental reimbursement is forty dollars per day. The next page says only with a certain endorsement, and for a maximum of twenty days. Retrieve only the first fragment, and the answer is confidently incomplete. So chunk along the boundaries of meaning, by section, with a little overlap.

Top k limits how many candidates are retrieved, and a similarity threshold discards weak matches. More context can add evidence, or distract the model.

Hybrid search combines lexical search, which preserves exact terms such as an endorsement code, with vector search, which finds matches in meaning. A reranker then reorders the shortlist.

Why keep vectors in PostgreSQL? For a moderate workload and a team that already runs it, vectors sit next to the metadata, the filters and the transactions. An approximate index trades a little recall for speed, and exact search is the quality baseline.

And to debug a wrong answer, walk the chain: source, parsing, retrieval, context, generation.

chapters.title: Tools, Agents & MCP
chapters.text:
Section six is tools, agents and the Model Context Protocol.

Start with who calls the service. In a fixed workflow, the backend decides. The user clicks Compare, Node validates the ids, calls the quote APIs, retrieves the evidence, scores in code, and asks the model only to explain. In an agentic workflow, the model chooses which tool to call next.

The tool calling loop runs like this. The backend sends the conversation and the schemas of the allowed tools. The model returns a tool request with a name and arguments. Your code validates the arguments, checks permission, runs the tool, and sends the result back. The model then either asks for another tool or writes the answer. So does the model actually call your API? No. It requests, and your code validates and executes.

The Model Context Protocol standardises how an AI application connects to servers that offer tools and data. It is useful when you want the same tools in several applications. It is not required for tool calling, and it is not retrieval.

Do you need an agent for comparison? No. A known sequence can be ordinary backend code. An agent earns its place when the next action depends on the model's interpretation of what the user wants.

For orchestration, pick the smallest thing that meets the requirement. A graph framework gives you explicit state, branches, persistence and the ability to pause, which is what human approval needs.

For approval, persist a checkpoint, show the proposed action to an authorised reviewer, and make the action idempotent, so approving twice does not act twice.

And to stop an agent from looping forever: bound the number of steps, the elapsed time and the tokens, detect repeated identical calls, and route to a person when it is not making progress.

chapters.title: Conversation & AI Features
chapters.text:
Section seven is conversation and other AI features.

Intent is harder than it looks. Health insurance, with a question mark, and I want health insurance could both mean the person wants help buying a policy. But the first could also be a request for a definition. Use the surrounding context, and ask a short clarifying question when it matters, instead of guessing.

To handle typos and different phrasings, map language into a small set of intents and extracted fields, validated against a schema. Then test equivalent phrases and misspellings against the same expected result.

Conversation state is more than chat history. Each turn of the user updates validated state on the backend: the intent, the collected fields, the selected quotes and any pending action. The chat log is for language context. The structured state is what the application acts on. A summary of the conversation is not a record of what the user agreed to.

The different features follow the same shape, authorised input, retrieval or tools, grounded generation and review, and each fails in its own way. Summarisation can drop or distort a fact, so keep references to the source. Generation needs a bounded task and a human review step. Intelligent search returns ranked documents or passages with their sources, where a chatbot returns a generated answer. And recommendations need a reason that a user can inspect.

The guide also sketches a roadmap from prototype to enterprise. Clarify the users, the journeys, what success means and how much failure is tolerable. Prototype one thin vertical slice with real contracts. Build an evaluation set early. Then harden it: security, monitoring, cost limits and a rollout plan.

chapters.title: React + LLM Integration
chapters.text:
Section eight is the React side, which is where a frontend candidate should be strongest.

Why not call the model directly from React? Because a browser cannot keep a secret. A server backed integration protects the provider credentials, and it gives you one place for identity, permissions, retrieval, budgets and logging. So React calls your route, and your route talks to the provider.

Model output flows one way, from server to browser. So HTTP streaming, usually with server sent event framing, fits well, and you seldom need a WebSocket. The real questions are about framing, authentication, cancellation and recovery after a disconnect. In practice, use the streaming helpers of an AI library on both sides, and do not write a fragile parser by hand.

Model the state of a request explicitly. Not a single loading flag, but named states: idle, submitting, retrieving, generating, complete, failed and cancelled. Give messages and runs stable ids, and update immutably.

The decisions about user experience matter as much as the plumbing. Show the user's message immediately. Show a meaningful status before the first token arrives. Offer a way to stop. Distinguish a tool that timed out from a search that found nothing. Render model output as text, and never as raw markup. And show sources.

To keep a chat interface fast, profile before memoising. Isolate the message that is streaming, so the rest of the list does not render on every token. Throttle the visual updates, and virtualise a long history.

For accessibility, use a real table for comparisons, visible focus, and a live region that announces status without reading every token aloud.

And testing has levels: unit tests for scoring and state transitions, component tests with a mocked stream, contract tests, a few end to end journeys, and evaluations for the model's output.

chapters.title: Prompts & Safety
chapters.text:
Section nine is prompts and safety.

A well structured, grounded prompt has clear parts. The role and the task. The rules, including what to do when the evidence is missing. The evidence itself, clearly delimited and marked as data. And the required shape of the output. But prompting supports controls. It cannot replace authorisation, business rules or validation of the output.

Each threat gets a concrete control, and a test that proves the control works.

Prompt injection. A document or a tool result contains text that reads like instructions. Treat everything retrieved as data. And keep tools on an allowlist, with permissions checked in code, so that even a fooled model cannot do anything the user was not allowed to do.

Data leaking between users. Derive the identity on the server, and enforce tenant and document filters in the query itself. Never rely on the prompt to keep data apart.

Personal information. Ask where it actually enters. A generic coverage document may contain none. But the user can type personal details, and a profile or quote tool can return them. Map every field, and send the model only what the task requires.

Validate the output twice. Structurally: the required fields, allowed values, the shape of ids, and an explicit state for unknown. And semantically: the selected quote really is one the user sent, the numbers match the systems of record, and every claim points at evidence that was retrieved.

Can retrieval eliminate hallucinations? No. Retrieval can return wrong or incomplete context, and generation can misread good evidence. So measure retrieval quality and answer quality separately.

A guardrail, then, is any control around inputs, retrieval, model behaviour, tool execution or outputs. The strongest ones are in code.

chapters.title: Evaluation & Tuning
chapters.text:
Section ten is evaluation and tuning.

Begin with precise wording, because it protects you in an interview. Changing chunk size, retrieval filters, prompts or top k is application tuning. Fine tuning means training the model's weights. If you are asked how you fine tuned it, and you did not, say so: I tuned the application, not the model.

A realistic improvement loop looks like this. Build a representative test set, with expected facts and source passages reviewed by someone who knows the domain. Include simple cases, ambiguous ones, conflicting documents, questions with no evidence at all, and adversarial ones. Run the system and separate two kinds of failure. If the right passage was not retrieved, fix extraction, metadata, chunking or search. If it was retrieved and the answer is still wrong, fix the prompt, the context assembly or the model. Change one thing, run the set again, and compare.

Know which metric answers which question. Recall at k: of all the relevant passages, what share appeared in the top k? Precision at k: of the k retrieved, what share were relevant? Faithfulness: does the answer stay within the evidence? And for operations: latency at the ninety fifth percentile, and cost for each successful task.

Should the model grade itself? Model assisted grading can scale evaluation. But calibrate it against human labels, and add deterministic checks for ids, numeric facts and permissions, which code can verify exactly.

When is fine tuning justified? For persistent behaviour, format or domain style, when a measured baseline with good prompts is not enough, and you have high quality examples.

Before release, run the labelled set, the safety cases and the cost and latency checks, and make that suite a gate in the pipeline.

chapters.title: Production
chapters.text:
Section eleven is production.

AI features fail in predictable ways, and each needs a recovery path and a metric. The provider returns a rate limit or a server error: retry with bounded backoff and jitter. One data source times out: return partial results, clearly marked. The stream disconnects: persist the state of the run, so the client can resume or fetch the result.

What do you log and trace? Follow the request from the browser, through the backend, retrieval, the model, the tools and back. Attach a run id, the model identifier, the prompt version, the retrieval index version, token counts and latencies for each stage. With versions recorded, you can explain why an answer changed between Tuesday and Wednesday. And keep personal data out of the logs.

Caching needs care. Embeddings for unchanged documents can be reused freely. But cache results only with keys that include the tenant, the authorisation scope, the policy version and the model and prompt versions. A cache key that forgets the tenant is a data leak.

When a response is slow, trace the latency of each stage before changing anything: authentication, retrieval, outside tools, time to the first token, and total completion. Then shorten the critical path. Run independent fetches together, trim the context, stream early, and use a smaller model where evaluation shows it is good enough.

To reduce cost, track input and output tokens, tool loops and retries per successful task. Route easy requests to a cheaper model, and cap the number of steps.

Where long jobs are involved, the pieces fit together like this. PostgreSQL owns the durable records. Redis holds short lived state. A queue carries the jobs. And server sent events push progress to the browser.

Release gates are the ordinary tests plus a fixed evaluation suite, with the prompt, the model and the tool schemas all versioned.

chapters.title: Tools, Providers & APIs
chapters.text:
Section twelve is tools, providers and APIs.

A sensible stack, and what each layer is for. React or Next.js with TypeScript for the interface and the backend for frontend. An AI library or the provider's own client for talking to the model and streaming. A schema library for validation at run time. PostgreSQL with a vector extension for application data and for search. And a tracing tool for observability.

The main providers differ less in what the models can do than in how you reach them. One offers its models directly. One offers the same family through a cloud platform, with that platform's identity, networking and regional controls. One has its own models and client library. And one is a cloud service that gives access to models from several vendors behind one API. In an enterprise, the choice often follows where the company's data and contracts already are.

Current API conventions differ from older tutorials. Parameter names, the way streams are produced and consumed, and even the recommended endpoints have changed across major versions. The guide records what it verified on a stated date, and treats those details as something to check again.

That leads to the most useful habit in this section: how to verify an API before you write code. Inspect the versions actually installed in the project and its lockfile. Read the migration guide for that major version. And type check the exact imports and calls, because the compiler will tell you at once when a tutorial is out of date.

Finally, data sources. Every scenario needs approved inputs, and a named owner who is responsible for keeping them fresh. An AI feature built on documents nobody owns will give stale answers.

chapters.title: React & Full-stack Essentials
chapters.text:
Section thirteen is React and full stack essentials, the fundamentals an interviewer will still probe, each tied to an AI product.

Effects are for synchronising with something outside React, such as a subscription, a timer or a stream, and they need a cleanup. In a chat interface, that means closing the stream when the component unmounts or the conversation changes. Effects are not for values you can calculate during render.

For state, the rule is scope, frequency and complexity. Local state for an isolated interaction. Lifted state when nearby components share it. Context for values that many components read and that seldom change. And a store when updates are frequent or the transitions are complex.

In TypeScript, the theme is that types exist at compile time and validation happens at run time. Use a discriminated union for the request states. Narrow unknown values before using them. And validate everything that arrives from the model or the network against a schema.

For a live coding round, clarify the input and output first, and what setup is available. Define minimal types and the states. Build the happy path, then loading, error and empty states, and say what you would test.

Say the architecture terms correctly. Node is a JavaScript runtime. TypeScript is a typed language that compiles to JavaScript. Express and NestJS are backend frameworks. Next.js is a React framework that also runs on the server.

On collaboration: clarify the acceptance criteria with product and design, agree the API and the stream contract with the backend engineers, and establish who owns the evaluation labels and the documents.

And with Tailwind, use utilities for spacing, type, responsive layout and focus states, and extract repeated patterns into components.

chapters.title: Answering Well
chapters.text:
The final section is about answering well, and it is short.

Use one structure for every technical answer. First the direct answer, in one sentence: I would use a deterministic comparison workflow with one explanation call. Then the mechanism, as a short sequence with named inputs and outputs: the backend loads exact facts, retrieves scoped evidence, applies the rules, and asks the model to explain. Then one concrete example. Then the trade off: what this costs, and when you would choose differently.

Direct answer, mechanism, example, trade off. It keeps an answer under two minutes, and it stops you from circling before you reach the point.

Keep answers technical by naming things. Say which component does what, what goes in and what comes out. The quote ids go in, and a validated explanation with source ids comes out, is stronger than the AI analyses the quotes.

Be precise about your own experience. Say built, when you built it. Say designed, or studied, when that is the truth. The worked example in this guide is practice material with invented data, so present it as how you would design such a feature, and not as something you shipped. Interviewers probe, and an inflated claim falls apart on the second question.

And prepare questions for the interviewer that show you are thinking about the work. Which AI features would I own first: the conversational interface, retrieval, agents or the frontend integration? Which provider and which backend contracts are already in place? How do you evaluate quality today, and who owns the test set? And what has been the hardest failure so far?

That is the guide. Say the forty five second architecture answer out loud once before you stop.
